speaker: Jonathan Gray
title: Blackstone's Jon Gray on real estate, rates, and building a winning company culture
question: In private markets, why do thematic investments often disappoint even when the underlying macro trend plays out?
guest: One of the challenges with thematic investing is a couple of challenges. One is you end up paying too high a price just because you get so enthused, or it's a bad business in a good neighborhood. The other thing is sometimes the neighborhood may change, right? There have been trends that have been really good, but then the technology changes something. So you've got to constantly be checking. I mean, one of the questions on data centers these days is, do you have a bubble? Is there too much capital going to it? There, fortunately, we think power is a real constraint, and you tend not to speculatively build a $2 billion data center. So the tenant demand creates a constraint as well. But you have to, as an investment organization, as much as you're leaning forward, constantly be questioning. Use streaming as an example, right? That was a really good area, production of content. I still think it's a long-term growth business, but there was too much capital, and we've seen a retrenchment now.

models.label: Claude Fable 5.2
models.answer:
Because being right about a trend is not the same as capturing its value. Several things tend to break the link between the two.

The main one is price. A widely recognised theme attracts capital quickly, so entry valuations already assume the growth; when the trend then plays out as expected, there is little left for returns, and multiples often compress on exit.

Capital also creates competition. Abundant funding finances many near-identical companies, which drives up customer acquisition costs and erodes margins. Industry growth then accrues to customers, or to incumbents and suppliers, rather than to the backed companies' equity holders. Railways, airlines, solar and much of cleantech 1.0 followed this pattern.

Timing matters too. Private funds have fixed lives of about ten years, and themes often take longer to mature than that, so investors can be forced to sell before the payoff arrives.

Finally, selection suffers. A thematic mandate creates pressure to deploy, so managers accept weaker companies with loose exposure to the theme, and funds raised at peak enthusiasm are concentrated in poor vintages.

In short, the trend drives revenue growth, but returns depend on entry price, competitive structure and timing.

models.label: Gemini Carbon
models.answer:
In private markets, thematic investments frequently underperform even when the macro thesis proves right because identifying a structural trend is far easier than capturing its economic surplus. Consensus themes attract a flood of capital, inflating entry valuations so heavily that years of best-case growth are priced in upfront, leaving returns vulnerable to multiple compression at exit. Simultaneously, abundant funding subsidizes dozens of competing entrants, driving up talent and customer acquisition costs while eroding pricing power and margins—meaning customers and suppliers, rather than equity holders, capture most of the value created.

Private market mechanics compound these hazards. Fixed fund lifecycles create unforgiving timing mismatches, where slower-than-expected adoption or closed exit windows can sink a directionally right thesis, as seen in early cleantech. Moreover, illiquidity locks investors into specific companies long before technological standards and competitive moats settle, turning broad macro convictions into fragile single-asset bets where incumbents or a tiny handful of power-law winners take the spoils while the median thematic deal disappoints.

models.label: Claude Opus 5.5
models.answer:
Thematic investments usually disappoint because being right about the trend is not the same as making money from it. When a theme like energy transition, AI, or aging populations becomes obvious, capital piles in. Lots of funds chase a limited set of investable companies, which pushes up entry valuations and compresses future returns. The good outcome is already in the price.

Second, the value a trend creates often doesn't go to the companies investors can actually buy. Competition, falling prices, customers, incumbents, or later entrants can capture it instead. Solar adoption boomed, for example, while many panel makers lost money.

Third, timing is unforgiving in private markets. Funds have fixed lives, so a trend that takes fifteen years to mature doesn't help a fund that has to exit in five to seven. Illiquidity also means investors can't easily adjust as the picture changes.

Finally, focusing on one theme concentrates risk and loosens discipline. Managers may relax underwriting, overpay for "strategic" assets, or back weaker teams just to get exposure. Returns ultimately depend on asset selection, entry price, and execution, not on whether the macro story comes true.

models.label: Gemini Neon
models.answer: In private markets, being right about a macro trend is rarely enough to generate strong returns because the link between industry growth and investor profits often breaks down. First, compelling themes attract floods of capital, driving up entry valuations as funds compete for the same limited pool of deals; paying too much upfront leaves little room for error or multiple expansion. Second, even when a theme succeeds, intense competition frequently erodes margins, and value tends to accrue to consumers, suppliers, or entrenched incumbents rather than the specific companies backed by private investors. Picking the eventual category winner early is notoriously difficult. Finally, illiquidity magnifies timing risk. Because private funds operate on fixed horizons and rely on receptive exit markets, arriving a few years too early—or needing to exit during a downturn—can turn a sound macro thesis into a poor investment. Ultimately, strong macro tailwinds cannot compensate for overpaying, weak unit economics, or misaligned timing.

models.label: GPT-6.2-Sol
models.answer:
A macro trend can play out exactly as expected and still disappoint investors. When a theme is popular, investors bid up entry valuations, so strong growth may already be priced in. The same enthusiasm funds new competitors, which can drive up costs and squeeze margins. And the companies that look like the clearest way to invest in the trend may capture little of the value it creates. The profits may accrue to suppliers, distributors, or customers.

Private markets add a timing problem. A company can run short of cash and dilute early investors before demand materializes. A fund may also need to sell while exit markets are weak. The return ultimately depends on how much cash the business can generate, what investors pay for it, and what they can realize at exit.

models.label: GPT-6.2-Astra
models.answer:
A theme can correctly predict where demand will grow and still be a poor guide to what a company is worth. In private markets, funds often chase the same limited set of deals, bidding up entry prices until they already assume years of rapid growth. Even a company that meets those expectations can deliver a weak return if the fund sells it at a lower valuation multiple.

The trend also says little about who keeps the profits. Competition may push the benefits toward customers, while the portfolio company spends heavily to expand and earns little on that capital. Timing matters, too: demand may arrive on schedule for the industry but too late for a fund that needs to exit. A sound thematic investment therefore requires a view on which company can turn growth into cash, how long that will take, and what price leaves room for an attractive return.
